extracted.intended_audience: writers of memoir and short fiction; writing students and literary readers interested in craft
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft guidance for writing memoir and short fiction, drawn from Tobias Wolff's conversation about voice, revision, memory, scene-making, and ethical boundaries in life-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt authentic child voice / resist adult hindsight
rubrics_metrics.description: “I had to give up the things I had learned from being a 10-year-old and become that unlearned 10-year-old again. I could not gift him with the kind of wisdom or insight that I really did not have at the time.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To write a convincing younger voice, re-create the naivete and limited understanding of that age rather than narrating with adult insight. Avoid retroactive explanations or moralizing that the child would not have possessed. Drawing on current interactions with children can help recapture that perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write without heat or hyperbole / plain truthful tone
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use understatement and an unadorned tone to convey brutality or emotional truth more powerfully than sensationalizing. Example: the scene of corporal punishment gains force because it is unvarnished rather than melodramatic. Anti-pattern: overwrought language that tells rather than shows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prune repetition; cut details that merely repeat the point
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave out material that simply repeats what you've already established; the first draft was much longer and required pruning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the psychological or moral pattern you want to show and remove additional incidents that only restate it. You can make the point once and strengthen the narrative by eliminating redundancy. Warning: avoid cutting so much that you remove structural 'muscle' or crucial elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize memoir as episodes / story-like incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: “The book is organized ... in episodes that are story-like. That's how I remembered my life.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure a memoir around signal incidents or episodes that form the blocks of memory; these discrete scenes can be assembled to build a sense of life. Use episodic organization when your memory naturally recalls events as discrete stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discover the book through drafting; revision is essential
rubrics_metrics.description: “You may have to just write your way toward that… you need to resign yourself not to writing the perfect draft right away, but to revision and look at yourself at these first drafts as a process of discovering.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect to learn what your book is about in the act of writing. Treat early drafts as exploratory and rely on revision to find the core truth or animating question. Practical tip: allow drafts to reveal the central problem rather than forcing a prespecified outline too early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't turn real people into mere symbols; show full complexity
rubrics_metrics.description: “I wasn't bending over backwards to be compassionate and loving with everybody... they were human and they had the full complement of human foibles and even virtues.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portray real people in their complexity rather than reducing them to single virtues or vices. Resist using acquaintances as flat symbols to make a point; recognize their mixed motives and humanity. This yields more truthful and ethically responsible memoir.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect factual bounds of memoir; don't invent events
rubrics_metrics.description: “What you can hold yourself to is not saying that things happened that didn't happen. If you are writing a memoir, you have at least that charge that you have to respect.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you label a work a memoir, avoid fabricating events. If you need to invent or alter facts, consider whether the piece should be fiction. Boundary rule: subjective reconstruction of memory is acceptable, but outright inventions that purport to be factual undermine memoir's contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge memory's subjectivity while seeking essential truth
rubrics_metrics.description: “Memory is never true, is it? On the other hand, it's the essential truth.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept that memory is subjective and selective; use the 'essential truth'—the psychological or emotional reality—rather than insisting on documentary precision. Still, distinguish between subjective recollection and fabrication; be transparent about limitations if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in scenes; use scene-making to learn and reveal
rubrics_metrics.description: “When you start to narrate life in scenes... I'm writing toward what I want to know, so I learn a lot in the crafting of a scene.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame life-writing around concrete scenes rather than general summary. Crafting scenes helps you discover detail, motive, and meaning. Scenes are a tool both for storytelling and for the writer's inquiry into what really happened or mattered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be generous to the reader; prioritize reader experience
rubrics_metrics.description: “Rule number one, which is about generosity to the reader, the reader's experience, of giving life with both hands, entertaining, eliciting our fear, our hopes.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to engage, entertain, and move readers: provide vivid life, emotional stakes, and clear patterns. Avoid withholding crucial context or being gratuitously obscure; consider how scenes land for a reader rather than only for the writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: In fiction, invent constraints for yourself amid freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: “Your freedom is absolute. I mean, when you have so much to choose from, so many ways to go, that is, you have to invent the constraints on yourself.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fiction offers boundless creative choices, which can be paralyzing. Establish self-imposed rules (point of view, scope, formal limits) to shape and focus the work. These constraints function as productive boundaries rather than restrictions on creativity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid moralizing; show rather than tell a character's development
rubrics_metrics.description: The book shows 'the making of a boy's moral compass moment to moment' rather than instructing the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate moral growth or deterioration through incidents and choices rather than summarizing or lecturing. Let the reader infer patterns from repeated actions and consequences instead of explicit commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use believable self-representation when inventing (ethical embellishment)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the anecdote about fabricating recommendation letters, he says he 'made no claims that seemed false to me' and wrote in 'the words my teachers would have used.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you embellish aspects of a self-portrait (tone, emphasis, selective memory), ground those choices in what feels believable to you as the narrator. Avoid outright falsehoods that would be unbelievable or ethically problematic in memoir contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize that narrativizing life can loop perception
rubrics_metrics.description: “When you start to pattern your life, does it create a kind of accelerating effect... a loop where you see more of what you already wrote because that's what you think has happened.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be mindful that arranging memory into stories can shape subsequent recollection and interpretation. Use corroboration, multiple perspectives, and disciplined revision to check narrative-driven bias; treat your narrative choices as interpretive acts, not neutral reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Perseverance and humility in craft: keep trying without over-measuring results
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Eliot: 'For us, there is only the trying. The rest is not our business.' Writing often feels precarious; keep working.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain discipline and persistence; accept that early drafts may feel inadequate. Don't obsess over immediate judgments of success; continual effort and revision produce durable work.
